📌 OTC Derivatives

OTC (Over-the-Counter) derivatives are privately negotiated financial contracts between two counterparties, rather than being traded on a centralized exchange.

🔹 Key Characteristics
• Customized to meet specific requirements
• Bilateral contracts between counterparties
• Governed by legal documentation such as the ISDA Master Agreement
• Higher counterparty credit risk, managed through collateral/CSA
• Can be linked to multiple underlying assets

🔹 Common Types
1️⃣ Interest Rate Derivatives – Swaps, Forwards, Options
2️⃣ Currency Derivatives – FX Forwards, Options, Cross-Currency Swaps
3️⃣ Credit Derivatives – CDS, Total Return Swaps
4️⃣ Equity Derivatives – Forwards, Options, Swaps
5️⃣ Commodity Derivatives – Forwards, Swaps, Options
6️⃣ Exotic/Structured Derivatives – Barrier, Cliquet, Quanto, etc.

🔹 Core Components
An OTC derivative typically defines the underlying asset, notional amount, maturity, payment frequency, day-count convention, payoff structure, counterparties and legal documentation.

🔹 Example – Interest Rate Swap
Two parties exchange interest-rate cash flows:
Fixed Rate ↔ Floating Rate, calculated on an agreed notional amount and generally settled periodically on a net basis.

🔹 OTC Derivative Lifecycle
Trade Initiation → Trade Capture → Confirmation → Valuation/MTM → Settlement → Termination/Expiry

🔹 Benefits
✅ Customization
✅ Flexible structures
✅ Effective hedging of complex exposures
✅ Efficient risk management

🔹 Key Risks
⚠️ Counterparty/Credit Risk
⚠️ Market Risk
⚠️ Liquidity Risk
⚠️ Operational Risk

💡 Key takeaway: OTC derivatives are an essential part of modern financial markets, helping banks, corporates, asset managers and other institutions manage risk, hedge exposures and create customized investment solutions.
